Intransigence is the quality of absolutely refusing to change your position, make a compromise, or even consider another point of view — no matter what is said, argued, offered, or proven to you. It is the state of being completely and deliberately unmovable.

It is not just resistance. It is total, sealed-off refusal.

Think of it this way: imagine two people trying to settle a dispute. One person listens, considers, and is willing to find middle ground. The other person has already decided, and nothing — no new evidence, no emotional appeal, no generous offer, no logical argument — will shift them even slightly. That second person is displaying intransigence.

What makes intransigence more than just stubbornness is the sense that the person is consciously and firmly holding their ground — often to a degree that others find unreasonable or frustrating. There is a certain rigidity to it, like a locked door with no key. It signals not just disagreement, but an active, determined refusal to engage with the possibility of being wrong or of yielding.

This is why intransigence often comes up in the context of negotiations, political conflicts, workplace disputes, and ideological standoffs — situations where the refusal to move has real consequences for everyone involved.
Is It Always a Negative Word?

Almost always, yes — but not quite always.

When used negatively (which is most of the time), intransigence is a criticism. It suggests that someone is being unreasonably rigid, that their stubbornness is causing harm, blocking progress, or making resolution impossible. For example: "The peace talks collapsed due to the government's intransigence." Here, the word places the blame squarely on their refusal to budge.

Occasionally, however, the word can carry a neutral or even quietly admirable tone — when someone is refusing to compromise on a matter of deep moral principle. A civil rights leader who refused to accept slow, token change could be described as showing intransigence — and history might view that refusal as courage, not obstruction. A scientist who refuses to accept bad data, no matter how much pressure they face, is being intransigent in a way that protects truth.

The key distinction: the word itself is neutral in definition, but in actual usage, it almost always implies that the observer finds the refusal excessive or harmful. If the refusal were clearly noble and principled, most people would reach for a different word — like resolve or conviction.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Stubbornness is the closest everyday cousin. But intransigence is more formal, more serious, and implies a more total and deliberate kind of refusal. You call a toddler stubborn. You call a political bloc intransigent.

Obstinacy is also close — it means persistently refusing to change one's mind despite good reasons to do so. Intransigence and obstinacy overlap, but intransigence more specifically suggests a refusal to engage in any negotiation or compromise whatsoever, while obstinacy can sometimes just mean clinging to a belief.

Inflexibility is milder — it describes someone who doesn't adapt easily. Intransigence is sharper: it implies not just inflexibility but active, firm resistance to any movement at all.

Here are the kinds of sentences you would genuinely find this word used in:

"Years of intransigence on both sides meant that the conflict had no end in sight."

"Her intransigence during contract negotiations cost the company a valuable partnership."

"Critics pointed to the committee's intransigence as the main reason the reform bill died."

"His intransigence on this single issue made him impossible to work with, even when everything else was agreed upon."

The adjective form is intransigent — used to describe a person or position: "He was completely intransigent." "Their intransigent stance frustrated everyone at the table."

Sometimes, rarely, you will see an intransigent used as a noun to refer to the person themselves: "The council was full of intransigents who refused every proposal."

If you want to carry this word with you in one sentence:

Intransigence is the absolute, unyielding refusal to change your position, compromise, or negotiate — no matter what arguments, evidence, or offers are presented to you.

Once you see it that way — a wall that won't move, a door that won't open — the word will always make sense in context.
